newsitem.title: POLAND: Gdansk shipyard workers block roads in protest.
newsitem.headline: Gdansk shipyard workers block roads in protest.

text.p: Almost 2,000 workers from the bankrupt Gdansk shipyard blocked tramlines and roads in the Baltic coast city on Wednesday, causing traffic chaos in a protest against losing their jobs.

The demonstrators set alight tyres and paint barrels on tram tracks during the morning, sending ominous plumes of dark smoke over the city while traffic jams stretched for many kilometres (miles) out of the city centre.

The yard's receiver announced last week that he would have to sack the remaining 3,800 workers at the yard which gave birth to the Solidarity trade union in 1980, and sell its assets off piecemeal rather than as a going concern.

Poland's government, led by former communists converted to market principles, has refused to subsidise the 60-percent state treasury-owned yard which was declared bankrupt last year under the burden of 415 million zlotys ($136 million) in debts. The government did offer partial loan guarantees, but only if a bank could be persuaded to lend it money to keep going until a strategic investor was found.
The receiver acted after Polish bank Pekao SA refused a $100 million loan for construction of five ships for a German shipowner, saying terms of the contract were unsatisfactory.

At a rally by the shipyard gates just before Wednesday's protest, the yard's deputy Solidarity chief angrily accused the left-dominated government of having offered false hopes to the enterprise in order to weaken protests over its collapse.
"The Communists have cheated us," said Karol Guzikiewicz, adding that the government should have announced the yard's liquidation when bankruptcy was declared last year.
"We have been guilty of one mistake -- we naively believed the communists when they said they wanted to save our shipyard," Guzikiewicz said.
The enterprise's workers said they were planning to block rail transport in Gdansk on Thursday.
Meanwhile, in Warsaw the National Committee of the Solidarity union gathered in Warsaw to discuss the shipyard and other matters.
Solidarity leader Marian Krzaklewski told the meeting he had asked the government for the necessary permission to raise funds for saving the yard through the sale of contribution coupons.
Solidarity hopes that if it can obtain 50 million zlotys ($16.6 million) in this way it can find an investor ready to add 100 million ($33.2 million) more to build ships.
Solidarity, which toppled communism in 1989, says the leftist coalition government has subsidised other state firms and is denying aid because of the yard's opposition links.
Solidarity has grouped rightist opposition parties in an alliance which is leading opinion polls and could beat the coalition at parliamentary polls due in September this year.

Even if Solidarity wins, the victory would come too late for the Gdansk shipyard, where Lech Walesa founded Solidarity as the first free union in the former Soviet bloc -- which went on to play a crucial role in toppling communist rule in 1989.
